question_text: How will you explain that medieval Indian temple sculptures represent the social life of those days?
topic: Temple sculpture as a social record
topics: Temple sculpture as a social record
customKeyPointers: A temple wall is a public record, not only a sacred image
Dress, work, dance and donors are carved beside the gods
The sculpture shows who paid and who was visible

points.text: A medieval temple was a public place, so its sculpture recorded more than worship.
Panels show musicians, dancers, soldiers, traders and ordinary dress of the time.
Donor couples and guild marks show who had the surplus to build.
Myths are told in the social costume of the age, so the sacred and the everyday sit on one wall.
The sculpture is a social document because the society that paid for the temple put itself on the stone.

question_text: Why did the armies of the British East India Company – mostly comprising of Indian soldiers – win consistently against the more numerous and better equipped armies of the then Indian rulers? Give reasons.
topic: Why Company armies kept winning
topics: Why Company armies kept winning
customKeyPointers: The Company army was paid and drilled; many rival armies were seasonal and divided
A paid, drilled army beat a seasonal host
Indian rulers were divided and often financed the Company
The win was organisational, not a matter of numbers

points.text: Company armies won less by being larger than by being a standing system.
Regular pay, a clear command and drill held the line when a ruler's host scattered after one reverse.
Rival Indian states rarely stayed united, and several subsidised the very army that later beat them.
The Company could borrow, replace losses and fight the next season; a court army often could not.
The consistent win was a better military organisation against a divided political field.

question_text: Why was there a sudden spurt in famines in colonial India since the mid-eighteenth century? Give reasons.
topic: Colonial famines after the mid-eighteenth century
topics: Colonial famines after the mid-eighteenth century
customKeyPointers: The spike is political, not only a run of bad rain
Revenue was collected even in a failed season
Grain moved to export and the town while the village starved

points.text: Famines rose after the mid-eighteenth century because the new state took grain and cash out and put little back.
High fixed revenue left no stock for a dry year.
Rail and export moved food to where it could be sold, not where people were hungry.
Common lands, local grain stores and a ruler's relief obligation weakened together.
Bad rain became mass death because the colonial economy had removed the old cushions.

question_text: Describe the characteristics and types of primary rocks.
topic: Primary rocks
topics: Primary rocks
customKeyPointers: Primary rock is the first rock, made from magma or lava
Texture depends on how fast the melt cooled
Intrusive and extrusive are the two types

points.text: Primary rocks are igneous rocks, formed when molten material cools.
Slow cooling underground gives large crystals, as in granite. Fast cooling at the surface gives fine grain, as in basalt.
Intrusive bodies (batholith, dyke, sill) and extrusive bodies (lava flow) are the two settings.
They are hard, crystalline, and usually without fossils, and they weather into the material of later rocks.
Type is fixed by where the melt cooled and how fast.

question_text: Discuss the meaning of colour-coded weather warnings for cyclone prone areas given by India Meteorological Department.
topic: Cyclone warnings
topics: Cyclone warnings
customKeyPointers: The colour is a level of action, not a decoration
Green means no threat, yellow means be aware
Orange means be prepared, red means act now

points.text: IMD's colours tell a cyclone-prone district how urgent the weather has become.
Green: no severe weather expected. Yellow: watch, and keep plans ready.
Orange: be prepared to move people and stop exposed work. Red: take action, including evacuation.
The code is tied to wind, rain and the sea, and it is updated as the cyclone track changes.
The colour is a shared instruction so that warning and response use the same word.

question_text: Discuss the natural resource potentials of 'Deccan Trap'.
topic: Resource potential of the Deccan Trap
topics: Resource potential of the Deccan Trap
customKeyPointers: The Trap is a basalt pile, not an empty plateau
Weathered basalt becomes the black soil of cotton
The rock holds groundwater in cracks, and also building stone

points.text: The Deccan Trap is a thick basalt sheet whose value lies in what weathering and cracking make of it.
Regur, or black cotton soil, is the weathered gift and the base of cotton and soybean.
Joints and vesicles store groundwater in an otherwise dry plateau.
Basalt is a building and road stone, and the associated belts carry manganese and other minerals.
The Trap's potential is a farm resource first, and a stone and water resource with it.

question_text: Examine the potential of wind energy in India and explain the reasons for their limited spatial spread.
topic: Why wind power stays in a few regions
topics: Why wind power stays in a few regions
customKeyPointers: The resource is large, but the good wind is local
A steady speed, not a high peak, makes a site pay
Land, the grid and a state policy decide where the mills stand

points.text: India has a large wind resource, but the sites that pay are concentrated.
Good wind is mainly the western coast, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka and parts of the peninsula, plus some ridges.
The Gangetic plain and much of the interior lack a steady speed above the cut-in of a turbine.
Land, a nearby grid and a state that buys the power further narrow the map.
The spread is limited because usable wind, land and the wire do not coincide everywhere.

question_text: Explore and evaluate the impact of 'Work From Home' on family relationships.
topic: Work from home and the family
topics: Work from home and the family
subTopics: Work from home and family life
customKeyPointers: The office entered the house and did not leave the clock
Care work, usually women's, became harder to see
The effect depends on space, the job and who else is at home

points.text: Work from home moved the job into the room where the family already lives.
Commuting time came back as shared time, and some fathers saw the day's care for the first time.
The same house erased the line between a meeting and a meal, so irritation rose where space was small.
School closure and housework piled onto the person already doing both, usually a woman.
The impact is mixed: more presence, and a new conflict over whose time the house belongs to.

question_text: How is the growth of Tier 2 cities related to the rise of a new middle class with an emphasis on the culture of consumption?
topic: Tier 2 cities and a consuming middle class
topics: Tier 2 cities and a consuming middle class
customKeyPointers: A new middle class wants the metro life without the metro rent
Malls, schools and clinics are both a cause and a sign
Consumption, not only industry, is pulling these towns

points.text: Tier 2 growth and a new middle class are feeding each other through a culture of buying.
Jobs in services, a campus and a cheaper house pulled families out of the metro and the village.
That class spends on a private school, a clinic, a brand and a weekend, which builds the town's visible economy.
The town then attracts the next family because those goods are now there.
The city is growing because a class that defines itself by consumption has chosen it.

question_text: Given the diversities among tribal communities in India, in which specific contexts should they be considered as a single category?
topic: When tribes are one category
topics: When tribes are one category
subTopics: Tribes as one category and as many
customKeyPointers: Tribes are not one culture
A single category is justified where the harm is shared
Land, forest rights and a constitutional status are such contexts

points.text: Tribal communities are diverse, so one category is right only where their situation is shared.
The Constitution's Scheduled Tribe status, protective land laws and the Forest Rights Act treat a common disadvantage.
Displacement by mines, dams and a weak hold on the forest is a shared political fact.
Language, clan, faith and economy differ enough that culture and development schemes should not use one design.
One category for rights and protection; many categories for life and custom.

question_text: The political and administrative reorganization of states and territories has been a continuous ongoing process since the mid-nineteenth century. Discuss with examples.
topic: Reorganisation of states since the mid-nineteenth century
topics: Reorganisation of states since the mid-nineteenth century
customKeyPointers: The map has been redrawn in every period, not once in 1956
Colonial provinces, partition and linguistic states are chapters of one process
Union territories show the process is still open

points.text: Redrawing the political map has been continuous since the colonial state started making provinces.
After 1857 the British merged, split and directly ruled units to make them governable.
1947 partitioned the map, and princely states were integrated into provinces and then into states.
The States Reorganisation of 1956, and later Gujarat, Haryana, the North-East, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Telangana and new Union territories, continued the same work.
Each round mixed language, tribe, region and the need for a smaller administration.
Reorganisation is not a finished event of 1956. It is how the Union keeps matching the map to how people live.

question_text: Discuss the main contributions of Gupta period and Chola period to Indian heritage and culture.
topic: Gupta and Chola contributions
topics: Gupta and Chola contributions
customKeyPointers: The Gupta age is remembered for a classical standard in art and Sanskrit
The Cholas are remembered for bronze, the temple and a sea-going culture
One set a form; the other scaled it in the south

points.text: The Gupta and Chola periods each left a standard that later Indian culture measured itself against.
Gupta court culture fixed a classical Sanskrit literature, the decimal place in common use, and a calm, idealised sculpture and painting, as at Ajanta's later phase.
The Gupta temple, though small, set the plan of the later northern shrine.
The Cholas built the great living temples of the Tamil country, the bronze Nataraja tradition, and a temple-centred public life.
Their sea links carried that culture, and a temple administration, across the Bay.
Gupta gave a classical form. Chola gave that religious culture its largest southern institutions.

question_text: Discuss the significance of the lion and bull figures in Indian mythology, art and architecture.
topic: Lion and bull in Indian art
topics: Lion and bull in Indian art
customKeyPointers: Both animals are signs of power, not only decoration
The lion becomes royal and later national
The bull is strength, fertility and Shiva's companion

points.text: The lion and the bull carry authority and fertility through Indian myth and stone.
On Indus seals and later pillars the bull is mass and endurance. Nandi at the Shiva shrine makes that endurance a devotee's posture.
The lion is the vahana of Durga and the mark of the king. Ashokan capitals, especially Sarnath, turned four lions into a state emblem that the Republic kept.
Temple gates, thrones and coinage use both so that a visitor reads power before reading a text.
The pair also marks directions and dynasties, so the animal is a political sentence.
Their significance is that Indian art makes power visible as an animal the public already understands.

question_text: What are the forces that influence ocean currents? Describe their role in fishing industry of the world.
topic: Ocean currents and world fisheries
topics: Ocean currents and world fisheries
customKeyPointers: Wind, the Earth's spin, density and the continents steer a current
A current moves heat and also nutrients
The great fisheries sit where water rises or mixes

points.text: Ocean currents are driven by wind, rotation, density and the shape of the basins.
Trade winds and westerlies drag the surface. The Coriolis force turns the flow. Cold, salty water sinks and warm water spreads.
Continents deflect the flow into gyres.
Upwelling along Peru, California, Namibia and the monsoon coasts lifts nutrients, so plankton and then fish concentrate there.
Warm and cold currents meeting, as off Japan and Newfoundland, do the same. A warm year such as El Niño can collapse that upwelling and the fishery.
Currents matter to fishing because they decide where the food of the fish is.

question_text: Describing the distribution of rubber producing countries, indicate the major environmental issues faced by them.
topic: Rubber regions and their environment
topics: Rubber regions and their environment
customKeyPointers: Natural rubber is a wet tropical crop
South East Asia holds most of the output
The plantation replaces forest and a mixed farm

points.text: Natural rubber grows where it is hot and wet all year, so production is bunched in a few tropical countries.
Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, India, Malaysia and parts of West Africa and southern China dominate.
Estates have replaced rainforest, especially in the islands, with a one-crop cover that holds little wildlife.
Clearing, slope planting and processing effluent damage soil and streams.
A falling price pushes smallholders to cut more forest or to intensify with chemicals.
The producing countries share one environmental problem: a valuable tree standing where a forest used to be.

question_text: Mention the significance of straits and isthmus in international trade.
topic: Straits and isthmuses in trade
topics: Straits and isthmuses in trade
customKeyPointers: A strait is a shortcut the sea already made
An isthmus is a barrier, until a canal cuts it
Whoever sits on the point has a political lever

points.text: Straits and isthmuses matter because trade bunches at a few narrow places.
Malacca, Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and Gibraltar shorten routes between oceans. A closure adds days and cost.
An isthmus blocks a sea route. Suez and Panama cut Suez and the American isthmus and rewrote shipping distances.
Ports, canals, fees and a naval presence grow at these points.
A political crisis at one strait is immediately a price and a supply crisis elsewhere.
Their significance is that geography forces world trade through a handful of doors.

question_text: Troposphere is a very significant atmospheric layer that determines weather processes. How?
topic: Why weather happens in the troposphere
topics: Why weather happens in the troposphere
customKeyPointers: Almost all the water and the weather sit in this lowest layer
Temperature falls with height, so air can rise and make cloud
The surface heats the layer from below

points.text: Weather is a troposphere process because that is where the air, the water and the heat from the ground meet.
Nearly all the mass of water vapour is here, so cloud, rain, fog and storm form here.
Temperature falls with height, which lets warm moist air rise, cool and condense.
Differential heating of land and sea drives wind, monsoon and cyclone inside this layer.
The tropopause stops most rising air, so these motions stay in a shallow band rather than the whole atmosphere.
The troposphere determines weather because it is the only layer thin, wet and unstable enough to do so.

question_text: Analyse the salience of 'sect' in Indian society vis-a-vis caste, region and religion.
topic: Sect beside caste, region and religion
topics: Sect beside caste, region and religion
customKeyPointers: A sect is a chosen path inside a larger religion
It can cut across caste and still be captured by caste
People live the sect more than they live the census category

points.text: A sect is the form in which many Indians actually practise a religion.
Bhakti, Sikh tradition in its early phase, and groups inside Hindu, Muslim, Jain and Buddhist life organise worship, food and marriage beyond a single text.
A sect can ignore caste in the shrine and still marry inside caste at home.
The same sect changes accent by region: language, saint and temple are local.
Against 'religion' as a large label, the sect is the unit people donate to, vote around and quarrel over.
Sect is salient because it sits between the large religion and the local caste, and people use it to move between them.

question_text: Are tolerance, assimilation and pluralism the key elements in the making of an Indian form of secularism? Justify your answer.
topic: An Indian form of secularism
topics: An Indian form of secularism
customKeyPointers: Indian secularism is not a wall between state and faith
Tolerance, assimilation and pluralism each do a different job
They are incomplete without equal citizenship

points.text: Yes. An Indian secularism was built more from living with many religions than from banning religion from public life.
Tolerance is the minimum: the neighbour's festival is not a threat.
Assimilation is the older social fact of borrowing food, saint and word, though it can also hide the smaller tradition.
Pluralism is the stronger claim: more than one way can be legitimate at the same time, and the state keeps a principled distance rather than a hostile one.
The Constitution adds an element these three do not guarantee: equal rights, so that a majority's tolerance is not the minority's only protection.
The three are key to the Indian form. Equal citizenship is what stops them becoming only a majority's good manners.

question_text: Elucidate the relationship between globalization and new technology in a world of scarce resources, with special reference to India.
topic: Technology, globalisation and scarce resources
topics: Technology, globalisation and scarce resources
customKeyPointers: New technology is both a child of globalisation and its tool
It can stretch a scarce resource or exhaust it faster
The relationship is a choice of which technology the shortage rewards

points.text: Globalisation spread new technology quickly, and that technology decides how a scarce resource is used.
A connected world moves capital, a design and a machine to wherever the resource or the wage is.
The same tool can save the resource, as with a better seed, a drip line or a cheaper solar panel, or consume it faster, as with a deeper borewell.
India imports both: the digital public system and the appetite of a new consumer class.
Scarcity of water, land and clean air means the technology India adopts is no longer a neutral upgrade.
Globalisation delivers the tool. Scarcity decides whether that tool is a saving or a rush.
